power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Academic meetings are central to sharing and discussing research, and key events for networking and community building.
Their design shapes interaction patterns and knowledge flow.

Drawing on insights from cultural evolution, we outline how meetings can be structured to reduce disciplinary echo chambers and to foster inclusive, interdisciplinary exchange and cumulative knowledge building.
Specifically, we aim to help scholars align intended outcomes with design choices through theory-informed guidance.

Cultural evolution offers tools for understanding how meeting formats shape information transmission, learning, and the persistence of ideas, and how design choices at all stages of the cultural evolutionary process act as selection pressures.

For example, meetings aimed at generating new ideas benefit from broad exposure to diverse perspectives and flexible interaction patterns, whereas meetings focused on consolidating knowledge rely on repeated interaction for refinement and alignment.

While few scholars organise large-scale conferences, many take on the role of organising symposia, workshops, or lab retreats, for which the framework we outline offers practical, goal-directed design principles.
Whether small lab group meetings, skill-training workshops, or multi-day conferences with several thousand attendees, academic meetings offer opportunities for exchange around a shared agenda.

Scientific progress and responses to global societal challenges rely on inclusive, interdisciplinary collaboration across diverse research communities and beyond academia (Norström et al. 2020 , Specht & Crowston 2022).
text.formatted: Scientific progress and responses to global societal challenges rely on inclusive, interdisciplinary collaboration across diverse research communities and beyond academia <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Norström et al. 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">, Specht & Crowston 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Academic meetings can support this collaboration and knowledge exchange through networking, with benefits that extend years beyond the event itself (Edwards et al. 2017).
text.formatted: Academic meetings can support this collaboration and knowledge exchange through networking, with benefits that extend years beyond the event itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Edwards et al. 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Because meetings are costly in time and travel, researchers expect them to be meaningful and efficient relative to the resources invested.
However, large conferences are discipline-specific and compartmentalise sub-fields and topics in parallel sessions, limiting exchange across research programmes.
Smaller meetings and workshops are often densely packed, leaving little room for informal socialising or reflective thinking.
Such constraints can compromise creativity and innovation, which require both necessity and opportunities for exploration (Greenbaum et al. 2019).
text.formatted: Such constraints can compromise creativity and innovation, which require both necessity and opportunities for exploration <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Greenbaum et al. 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This combination of scientific demands and the constraints faced by time-pressed, resource-limited researchers presents a timely opportunity to rethink how academic meetings are organised.
This need is compounded by the fact that many such meetings are organised by academics themselves, who rarely have any formal training in event management.
Existing guides provide valuable advice on the logistics and management of events, including academic meetings.
For example, Corpas et al. (2008) outline ten rules focused on planning covering budgeting, time management, coordinating committee members, and collecting post-conference feedback.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Corpas et al. (2008)</ref> outline ten rules focused on planning covering budgeting, time management, coordinating committee members, and collecting post-conference feedback.

text.text: A Best Practices guide produced by a collaborative cross-disciplinary community of evolution researchers (NESCent 2012) emphasises leadership, group dynamics, clear agendas, effective breakout groups, and thoughtful participant recruitment.
These guidelines remain important for ensuring well-run events.
Here, we turn our attention to how the design of academic meetings affects social dynamics and learning outcomes.

Drawing on research in cultural evolution, social learning, and network science, we outline theory-informed design principles that foster innovation, effective learning, and the spread of rigorous scientific practices.

Cultural evolution is a theory of culture change focused on how behaviours, knowledge, norms, and practices are generated, transmitted, and accumulated across populations (Boyd & Richerson 1985; Mesoudi 2016).
text.formatted: Cultural evolution is a theory of culture change focused on how behaviours, knowledge, norms, and practices are generated, transmitted, and accumulated across populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Boyd & Richerson 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Mesoudi 2016)</ref>.

text.text: New information or behavioural variants can arise through various mechanisms, such as trial-and-error discovery or copying error (Perry et al. 2021).
text.formatted: New information or behavioural variants can arise through various mechanisms, such as trial-and-error discovery or copying error <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Perry et al. 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We use innovation to refer to the process of introducing novel cultural variants, regardless of whether they arise through asocial or social processes, deliberate or accidental, by de novo creation, recombination, or improvement of existing forms, and irrespective of whether they subsequently spread or persist (cf. Fogarty et. al 2015).
text.formatted: We use innovation to refer to the process of introducing novel cultural variants, regardless of whether they arise through asocial or social processes, deliberate or accidental, by de novo creation, recombination, or improvement of existing forms, and irrespective of whether they subsequently spread or persist (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Fogarty et. al 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Cultural variants can then spread through social learning , defined as the acquisition of information or skills by observing or interacting with others or their products (Heyes 1994).
text.formatted: Cultural variants can then spread through social learning , defined as the acquisition of information or skills by observing or interacting with others or their products <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Heyes 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Transmission is not random; because cognitive resources such as attention and memory are limited, people rely on selective social learning strategies to decide what, when, and from whom to learn (Kendal et al. 2018; Laland 2004).
text.formatted: Transmission is not random; because cognitive resources such as attention and memory are limited, people rely on selective social learning strategies to decide what, when, and from whom to learn <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kendal et al. 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Laland 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Cultural variants that are instrumentally or socially adaptive are most likely to be selectively transmitted, eventually stabilising to become part of a community's cultural repertoire.

Cultural evolutionary theory is consistent with, and complementary to, observations from events management, a broad field covering topics such as festivals and tourism, as well as academic meetings (Rogers & Wynn-Moylan 2023; Mair & Whitford 2013).
text.formatted: Cultural evolutionary theory is consistent with, and complementary to, observations from events management, a broad field covering topics such as festivals and tourism, as well as academic meetings <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Rogers & Wynn-Moylan 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Mair & Whitford 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Research shows how event design and social interactions can impact both individual experiences (Neuhofer et al. 2024; Crowther et al. 2018) and collective innovation (Maskell et al. 2006; Zhong & Luo 2018).
text.formatted: Research shows how event design and social interactions can impact both individual experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Neuhofer et al. 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Crowther et al. 2018</ref>) and collective innovation <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Maskell et al. 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Zhong & Luo 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Events are increasingly designed for transformative personal experiences and learning which extends beyond the immediate event, for example, by considering the choice of facilitators and venue (e.g., contact with nature; Neuhofer et al. 2024).
text.formatted: Events are increasingly designed for transformative personal experiences and learning which extends beyond the immediate event, for example, by considering the choice of facilitators and venue (e.g., contact with nature; <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Neuhofer et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Organisers may use play to help break down power structures and encourage participants to share their perspectives and co-create knowledge (Crowther et al. 2018).
text.formatted: Organisers may use play to help break down power structures and encourage participants to share their perspectives and co-create knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Crowther et al. 2018)</ref>.

text.text: At the collective level, business events such as trade fairs bring firms and competitors together to see and compare new products and interact with customers and suppliers.
These temporary clusters facilitate network building and knowledge exchange (Maskell et al. 2006), and can promote innovation and imitation (Zhong & Luo 2018).
text.formatted: These temporary clusters facilitate network building and knowledge exchange <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Maskell et al. 2006)</ref>, and can promote innovation and imitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Zhong & Luo 2018)</ref>.

text.text: From a cultural evolutionary perspective, these processes can be understood as the generation, transmission, and selection of cultural variants.
Building on this work, here we treat academic meetings as goal-directed cultural systems, where knowledge and norms are diffused along social pathways.
We argue that thoughtful design choices can actively shape cultural evolutionary dynamics.

To do so, we synthesise theoretical and empirical insights from cultural evolution to guide the planning of scientific meetings that support effective information transmission, and create learning environments where new ideas can emerge and persist.
We structure our argument tracing a simple cultural evolutionary pipeline from variation generation to transmission and stabilisation.

Accordingly, we call attention to (1) interaction patterns that promote innovativeness, (2) the social learning mechanisms that govern information transmission, and (3) how organisers can intentionally stabilise collective outcomes.
Throughout, we translate theory into concrete design recommendations for meeting organisers.

While these are often already intuitively implemented to varying degrees, and are discussed in the event management literature, here we link them explicitly to a cultural evolutionary framework in order to clarify the mechanisms by which design choices contribute to knowledge building.

We end by arguing that our framework is not only useful for organisers of academic meetings, but also for cultural evolutionary researchers who may consider meetings both as model systems and as sites for field experimentation.
Large-scale international scientific conferences emerged in the nineteenth century alongside improved travel infrastructure.

Historical accounts highlight their role as venues for both formal and informal communication, and the importance of face-to-face interactions in shaping how knowledge is created, shared, and refined (Bigg et al. 2023).
text.formatted: Historical accounts highlight their role as venues for both formal and informal communication, and the importance of face-to-face interactions in shaping how knowledge is created, shared, and refined <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bigg et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: By bringing researchers together, meetings facilitate rapid, high-fidelity transmission of information through social interactions (Lewis & Laland 2012).
text.formatted: By bringing researchers together, meetings facilitate rapid, high-fidelity transmission of information through social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lewis & Laland 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond knowledge exchange, academic meetings served multiple purposes from the outset, including community building and establishing shared standards.

For instance, in the late eighteenth century, the French government convened an international body of scientists to review the reliability of measurements used to support the metric system (Alder 2012).
text.formatted: For instance, in the late eighteenth century, the French government convened an international body of scientists to review the reliability of measurements used to support the metric system <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alder 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Today, conferences and workshops continue to establish consensus and field-unifying conceptual or methodological frameworks (Osterhammel 2009).
text.formatted: Today, conferences and workshops continue to establish consensus and field-unifying conceptual or methodological frameworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Osterhammel 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Academic meetings also curate exposure and endorsement.
Whereas early disciplinary conferences often aimed to represent entire fields, smaller and selective meetings emerged to foster focused discussions and convergence.
For example, the 836 attendees of the 1900 physics congress in Paris reportedly brought together over half of all professionals in the field at that time (Nye 1984).

text.text: Choices about invited speakers affect which ideas and practices gain visibility at academic meetings today.
Together, these functions position academic meetings as intentional settings where field-wide knowledge and norms are stabilised, while new ideas and frameworks are generated.

In the following sections, we unpack the goal-process-outcomes links and consider trade-offs in design decisions and mitigation strategies to help organisers choose interventions suited to their desired outcomes.
Cultural evolution depends on the introduction of novel variants.
Scientific meetings can facilitate this process by creating opportunities for diverse ideas to emerge and converge.
This section explores how diversity and inclusion of participants, and shaping their interactions can maximise innovation.
Across domains, diversity has been shown to benefit innovativeness and adaptability.

For example, heterogeneous groups outperform homogenous ones in problem-solving (Hong & Page 2004); diverse cities are more economically productive (Bettencourt et al. 2014); and policies that restrict diversity, such as immigration quotas, reduce rates of innovation (Moser & San 2020; Posch et al. 2025).
text.formatted: For example, heterogeneous groups outperform homogenous ones in problem-solving <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hong & Page 2004)</ref>; diverse cities are more economically productive <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bettencourt et al. 2014)</ref>; and policies that restrict diversity, such as immigration quotas, reduce rates of innovation <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Moser & San 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Posch et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In scientific contexts, diversity improves innovation and collective problem-solving (Wu et al. 2023).
text.formatted: In scientific contexts, diversity improves innovation and collective problem-solving <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Wu et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Two forms are particularly relevant: diversity in disciplinary background, which introduces variety in theoretical and methodological approaches, and diversity in lived experiences, which can highlight blind spots and challenge assumptions.
Meeting organisers can broaden participation by reducing barriers of attendance for underrepresented researchers.

Measures include providing accessibility and funding support, extending reach through remote participation and online engagement (Raby et al. 2022), and signalling a welcoming environment for scholars of diverse backgrounds (Walters & Higgins-Desbiolles 2025).
text.formatted: Measures include providing accessibility and funding support, extending reach through remote participation and online engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Raby et al. 2022)</ref>, and signalling a welcoming environment for scholars of diverse backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Walters & Higgins-Desbiolles 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, diversity among participants does not automatically translate into innovation.

Productive engagement in diverse groups requires sufficient social connectivity to ensure repeated interaction and recombination across differences (Schimmelpfenning et al. 2021; Baumann et al. 2024).
text.formatted: Productive engagement in diverse groups requires sufficient social connectivity to ensure repeated interaction and recombination across differences <ref type="bibr">(Schimmelpfenning et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baumann et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, increasing diversity introduces coordination problems; the underlying norms, assumptions, and terminology used in one discipline may not be shared by others, leading to misunderstandings.
Finally, diversity among participants does not guarantee that all perspectives are voiced or carry equal influence (Chen et al. 2025).
text.formatted: Finally, diversity among participants does not guarantee that all perspectives are voiced or carry equal influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Chen et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, gender dynamics can result in women's opinions being underrepresented while men ask a disproportionate number of questions (Carter et al. 2018).
text.formatted: For instance, gender dynamics can result in women's opinions being underrepresented while men ask a disproportionate number of questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Carter et al. 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Practical interventions can support equitable active engagement.
For example, organisers can diversify conveners (Casadevall & Handelsman 2014) and actively invite contributions during discussions (Carter et al. 2018).
text.formatted: For example, organisers can diversify conveners (Casadevall & Handelsman 2014) and actively invite contributions during discussions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Carter et al. 2018)</ref>.

text.text: To help participants navigate disciplinary differences, organisers can explicitly communicate norms and expectations through a code of conduct, and establish shared language by circulating foundational readings or providing working definitions for key terms.
Diversity can be structured dynamically over time, for example by varying how long different ideas are allowed to coexist.

Zollman (2010) introduced the concept of transient diversity to describe a dynamic in which high diversity in exploratory phases is followed by consolidation, when ideas are developed into concrete implementations. Smaldino and colleagues (2024) identified transient diversity as a general principle for collective problem solving.
text.formatted: Zollman (2010) introduced the concept of transient diversity to describe a dynamic in which high diversity in exploratory phases is followed by consolidation, when ideas are developed into concrete implementations. <ref type="bibr">Smaldino and colleagues (2024)</ref> identified transient diversity as a general principle for collective problem solving.

text.text: They argue that it can be fostered by increasing initial diversity of perspectives and problem-solving strategies, while strategically limiting early information flow to allow subgroups to explore a range of different options before comparing them.
Network connectivity also plays an important role for collective problem-solving, by affecting how ideas spread between individuals and subgroups.
Fully connected groups tend to easily and rapidly converge on solutions, but risk premature consensus on suboptimal ones.

In contrast, partially connected or modular networks allow parallel exploration and are more likely to produce diverse and high-quality solutions to complex problems (Lazer & Friedman 2007; Mason et al. 2008; Derex & Boyd 2016).
text.formatted: In contrast, partially connected or modular networks allow parallel exploration and are more likely to produce diverse and high-quality solutions to complex problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lazer & Friedman 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Mason et al. 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Derex & Boyd 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Occasional mixing between subgroups allows ideas to be combined and refined, potentially leading to globally optimal solutions.
For example, Derex and Boyd (2016) showed that partially connected groups were faster than fully connected groups in discovering the remedy to a virus in an experimental task.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Derex and Boyd (2016)</ref> showed that partially connected groups were faster than fully connected groups in discovering the remedy to a virus in an experimental task.

text.text: Similarly, Kline and Boyd (2010) found that Oceanic societies with more inter-island contact had more tool types than expected for their population size, suggesting that inter-group contact supports the emergence of more solutions.

text.text: Weak ties connect otherwise distant clusters of well-connected individuals; this helps information spread efficiently, and introduces non-redundant information (Granovetter 1973), with consequences for economic outcomes (Pfeffer & Parra 2009) and norm change (Miu & Colleran 2025).

text.text: However, some information requires reinforcement from multiple independent sources rather than a single exposure, a process called complex contagion (Firth 2020).

text.text: In these cases, diffusion depends on whether groups are linked by overlapping connections that can provide social affirmation, i.e. 'wide' bridges across a network (Centola & Macy 2007).

text.text: Modularity addresses this trade-off between reach and reinforcement by enabling parallel connections in largely separated groups, which improves transient diversity and collective problem solving (Schilling & Steensma 2001; Gomez & Lazer 2019; Smaldino et al. 2024).

text.text: Academic meetings can complement transient diversity by providing occasional mixing between otherwise separate subcommunities.
Once groups have explored different approaches in parallel, meetings allow new approaches to be compared, combined, and refined.
Meetings also create weak ties between scholars who would otherwise be unlikely to meet.
For example, Chai and Freeman (2019) found that participating in small scientific conferences can lead to collaborations and citations among scientists who were not previously associated.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Chai and Freeman (2019)</ref> found that participating in small scientific conferences can lead to collaborations and citations among scientists who were not previously associated.

text.text: Formats that foster repeated contact are especially valuable, such as thematic gatherings, early-career mixers, extended coffee breaks, and buddy systems that pair volunteers with newcomers.

To keep these opportunities accessible, organisers should avoid limiting social events to evenings or centering them on alcohol, since both can exclude attendees with caregiving duties or those who do not drink.
Daytime alternatives such as excursions or social lunches can broaden participation.

It is important to note, however, that groups characterised by lower connectivity take longer to converge onto shared knowledge (Segovia-Martin et al. 2020) and can generate clustered networks of specialists if groups are not sufficiently interconnected (Smolla & Akçay 2019).
text.formatted: It is important to note, however, that groups characterised by lower connectivity take longer to converge onto shared knowledge <ref type="bibr">(Segovia-Martin et al. 2020</ref>) and can generate clustered networks of specialists if groups are not sufficiently interconnected <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Smolla & Akçay 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Further, scheduling too much unstructured social time can lead to participant disengagement, tangential discussions, and can reinforce established networks when participants mix with known collaborators rather than new colleagues.
Mitigating these risks therefore requires a combination of tight clusters with repeated connections and periodic recombination across groups, followed by a final consolidation phase.
This can be achieved by combining independently working breakout groups with deliberate recombination of participants or synthesis sessions.
Themed working breaks, such as encouraging participants to discuss a central topic or shared problem over coffee, can maintain focus while promoting exploratory exchange.
Allocating time at the start of subsequent structured sessions for sharing ideas discussed over informal breaks can further promote cross-disciplinary conversations.
Creating opportunities for interaction among diverse participants is the first step in exposure to new ideas, and subsequent processes of transmission, refinement, and accumulation.
In this section we focus on transmission as a structured, non-random process.
Cultural knowledge can be transmitted vertically (from parents), oblique (non-parental adults), and horizontally (from peers) (Cavalli-Sforza & Feldman 1981; Hewlett et al. 2011).
text.formatted: Cultural knowledge can be transmitted vertically (from parents), oblique (non-parental adults), and horizontally (from peers) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cavalli-Sforza & Feldman 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hewlett et al. 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In academic training contexts, vertical transmission can be conceived of as occurring from advisors or principal investigators, oblique transmission as occurring from senior mentors or collaborators, and horizontal transmission as occurring within research groups, cohorts, or peer communities.

Vertical and oblique transmission are particularly effective for establishing and maintaining complex skills and norms, leading to uniform and persistent knowledge, while horizontal transmission facilitates exposure to new ideas and the rapid spread of these novel variants (Miu & Colleran 2025).
text.formatted: Vertical and oblique transmission are particularly effective for establishing and maintaining complex skills and norms, leading to uniform and persistent knowledge, while horizontal transmission facilitates exposure to new ideas and the rapid spread of these novel variants <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Miu & Colleran 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Transmission outcomes further depend on interaction frequency, task complexity, and learning strategies.

While simple information can spread through single encounters, complex skills or normative knowledge typically require repeated interactions (Centola & Macy 2007), often supported by imitation or teaching (Castro & Toro 2014).
text.formatted: While simple information can spread through single encounters, complex skills or normative knowledge typically require repeated interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Centola & Macy 2007)</ref>, often supported by imitation or teaching <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Castro & Toro 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Social learning strategies that are particularly relevant in academic contexts are prestige bias, whereby individuals preferentially attend to and copy those who are deferred to by others (Henrich & Gil-White 2001; Henrich & Broesch 2011; Jiménez & Mesoudi 2019), and conformist bias, which leads to individuals disproportionately copying the majority of the population as their behaviours are perceived as common or normative (Boyd & Richerson 1985; Morgan & van Leeuwen 2024).
text.formatted: Social learning strategies that are particularly relevant in academic contexts are prestige bias, whereby individuals preferentially attend to and copy those who are deferred to by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Henrich & Gil-White 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Henrich & Broesch 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Jiménez & Mesoudi 2019)</ref>, and conformist bias, which leads to individuals disproportionately copying the majority of the population as their behaviours are perceived as common or normative <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Boyd & Richerson 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Morgan & van Leeuwen 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These biases shape attention, learning, and retention, and influence which ideas and practices become dominant.

In sum, learning outcomes depend jointly on interaction patterns (who interacts with whom, and how often) and on the rules governing transmission (e.g., vertical or horizontal, simple or complex contagion, one-to-many or one-to-one, prestige or conformity bias).
Academic meeting formats should align transmission pathways with intended outcomes.

For example, one-to-many formats (e.g., talks, plenary sessions) are suited for broad knowledge dissemination and can increase the visibility of research, as reflected in paper citations and downloads (Leite Lopez de Leon & McQuillin 2020).
text.formatted: For example, one-to-many formats (e.g., talks, plenary sessions) are suited for broad knowledge dissemination and can increase the visibility of research, as reflected in paper citations and downloads (Leite Lopez de Leon & McQuillin 2020).

text.text: Sharing asynchronous materials such as recordings can further extend reach.
Keynote speakers, plenary panels, and session chairs are positions of prestige.

By inviting scholars who embody the scientific practices organisers aim to promote (e.g., Open Science practices, interdisciplinarity, or new methods), one-to-many formats paired with prestige biased social learning can ensure the proliferation of these practices.

In contrast, when the goal is to develop specific skills, workshops should combine high-fidelity transmission and supervised individual practice, a strategy that has been suggested to be critical for reliable skill acquisition and cumulative culture (Aoki et al. 2012).
text.formatted: In contrast, when the goal is to develop specific skills, workshops should combine high-fidelity transmission and supervised individual practice, a strategy that has been suggested to be critical for reliable skill acquisition and cumulative culture <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aoki et al. 2012)</ref>.

text.text: When working in isolation, each of these goals and design choices come at a cost.
One-to-many formats are unlikely to ensure the depth and durability of knowledge transfers.
Workshops, on the other hand, require small group formats, and thus, have limited reach.

Mixed designs can overcome these costs by pairing small-group sessions that support collaborative sense-making with plenary talks or cross-disciplinary panels that expand exposure across disciplinary boundaries.
Participants may bring different expectations to the same event and engage differently with these formats.
For example, an early-career researcher may prioritise broad overviews and learning about the norms of their field, while others may seek exposure to new ideas.

Accounting for such differences by clearly signalling meeting or session aims and offering formats that target different outcomes in parallel helps reduce mismatches between outcomes and attendee expectations.
Beyond exchanging research ideas, academic meetings are key sites where normative standards of interaction, visibility, and evaluation are enacted and reinforced.
This section focuses on dynamics that shape which practices persist over time.
Cultural accumulation depends on norms and institutions which shape shared expectations and behaviour (Currie et al. 2021; Chudek & Henrich 2011).
text.formatted: Cultural accumulation depends on norms and institutions which shape shared expectations and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Currie et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chudek & Henrich 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Many aspects of meetings (e.g., when to ask questions, turn-taking in discussions, how decisions are reached) are best understood as coordination problems, where the challenge is aligning behaviour rather than overcoming competing individual interests.
Disagreement, norm violations, or interpersonal conflict due to heterogeneity in preferences or individuals' influence can hinder coordination (Gavrilets et al. 2016).
text.formatted: Disagreement, norm violations, or interpersonal conflict due to heterogeneity in preferences or individuals' influence can hinder coordination <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gavrilets et al. 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction matters because coordination and cooperation fail for different reasons and require different solutions.

Cooperation requires individuals to pay a personal cost for collective benefit, and thus depends on incentives and enforcement; In academia, many core practices of knowledge-building rely on interaction norms and are not governed by formal rules; for example, how disagreement is expressed, whose contributions are taken seriously, or how credit is allocated.
When aiming to consolidate knowledge and produce a shared output, norms should be actively shaped with incentives or enforcement mechanisms.
Because consensus is not always achievable or efficient, meetings benefit from structured procedures for decision-making (e.g., majority voting) and conflict management.
Recent scholarship suggests that codes of conduct are not the norm across academic societies (Foxx et al. 2019; Lu & Webb Williams 2024).
text.formatted: Recent scholarship suggests that codes of conduct are not the norm across academic societies <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Foxx et al. 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Lu & Webb Williams 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, providing a code of conduct that specifies roles and responsibilities alongside mechanisms for intervention and enforcement, helps maintain coordination and effective transmission.

Organisers and session chairs can also promote norms by signaling which standards, values, or practices are endorsed by the community, by managing discussions and evaluating interactions to ensure inclusive and respectful participation (Carter et al. 20219), or by deciding whose contributions receive recognition (e.g., awards).
text.formatted: Organisers and session chairs can also promote norms by signaling which standards, values, or practices are endorsed by the community, by managing discussions and evaluating interactions to ensure inclusive and respectful participation <ref type="bibr">(Carter et al. 20219)</ref>, or by deciding whose contributions receive recognition (e.g., awards).

text.text: Norms can be refined over time through feedback, for example through shared notes, anonymous suggestion boxes, or follow-up discussions.
Such iterative design mirrors processes of cumulative cultural evolution and contributes to community building by allowing norms to persist, adapt, and accumulate.
When consistently upheld and enforced by organisers, chairs, and participants, these norms become stabilising institutions.
Importantly, setting strong norms can produce clusters of specialists with limited exposure to new ideas and reduced uptake of new skills (Smolla & Akçay 2019).
text.formatted: Importantly, setting strong norms can produce clusters of specialists with limited exposure to new ideas and reduced uptake of new skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Smolla & Akçay 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In scientific communities, such ' echo chambers ' have been associated with lower robustness and replicability (Danchev et al. 2019).

text.text: For academic events, organisers should aim to carefully balance consolidation and exploration: interaction structures must support coordination and transmission while preserving sufficient diversity and modularity to enable parallel exploration and innovation.
Deliberately including participants from closely related fields may introduce sufficient diversity to maintain exploration without jeopardising consensus building.

Similarly, structuring events as adversarial collaborations (Rakow 2022), where researchers with different views on a scientific question collaborate, can also drive progress towards rigorous consensus building.

text.text: While in the present paper we separated cultural evolutionary processes analytically to clarify mechanisms and derive theory-informed, actionable recommendations, we recognise that meeting design choices affect multiple goals, processes, and outcomes simultaneously.

Cultural evolutionary research, however, tends to investigate one mode or strategy of cultural transmission in isolation or, very rarely, compare social learning strategies (Atkisson et al., 2012; Deffner et al., 2020; Miu & Morgan 2020).

text.text: Rarely do studies investigate when and how social learning strategies might be traded off against each other.
Our exercise in translating cultural evolutionary theory into practical guidance emphasises the importance of considering cultural transmission not in isolation, but in realistic contexts.
Individuals and groups rationally and flexibly trade-off learning strategies (Kendal et al. 2018; Miu et al. 2020).

text.text: Understanding the conditions under which they do so will contribute to fundamental cultural evolution work.
Because academic meetings shape cultural transmission by structuring networks and learning opportunities, they lend themselves to testing theoretical predictions about social learning and innovation.

For example, academic events could be used to investigate how short-term network rewiring alters information diffusion and long-term collaboration in scientific communities; the role of prestige cues; or how unstructured networking and formal content sharing (e.g., talks) differ in outcomes.

text.text: Academic meetings are cultural systems in which network structure shapes diversity and transmission, while coordination and selection processes determine how ideas move, who is copied, and which behaviours and practices persist.
Throughout the paper, we have argued that organisers can deliberately shape meetings through three cultural evolutionary processes.
First, designers can cultivate a diverse pool of ideas, since variation underpins innovation and collective problem-solving.
Second, they can influence how knowledge is transmitted, and so which ideas gain traction.
Third, they can stabilise ideas and norms over time, supporting the accumulation and persistence of knowledge.

Thinking explicitly about these dynamics helps organisers recognise trade-offs between generating new ideas and consolidating existing knowledge, and between breadth and depth of the knowledge produced (Derex 2022).
text.formatted: Thinking explicitly about these dynamics helps organisers recognise trade-offs between generating new ideas and consolidating existing knowledge, and between breadth and depth of the knowledge produced <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Derex 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, effective meeting design begins with identifying a focal goal beyond mere content delivery, and aligning formats accordingly.
To help organisers, in Table 1 we summarised how the cultural evolutionary principles translate into concrete design choices for academic meetings, linking goals, mechanisms, and expected outcomes.

text.text: We foreground goals because many academic meetings are organised by researchers who have specific outputs in mind, such as a joint paper, an edited volume, or the uptake of a specific methodological innovation.

Meetings aimed at maximising innovativeness benefit from broad exposure, transient diversity, and modular networks with weak ties, whereas meetings focused on consolidation require repeated interaction, high-fidelity transmission, and coordination norms.
Large conferences usually combine several goals in parallel sessions, and different stakeholders, such as funders, host institutions, and attendees, may hold competing objectives.

In such cases, our framework can be applied at the level of individual sessions or formats, and can be used to identify tensions between them (e.g., prestige-driven plenaries may dampen the diversity that subsequent parallel breakouts aim to foster).
When organisers identify and communicate intended goals, participants and other stakeholders (e.g., session chairs) can decide whether it fits their aims and attend accordingly.

Although relatively few researchers organise large, recurring conferences, the theory-informed recommendations outlined above can also support the design of symposia, workshops, summer schools, or lab retreats.
Across scales, meetings face similar coordination challenges and rely on interaction norms and selective stabilisation to support cumulative knowledge building.

Online meetings can reproduce some features of in-person interactions, for example through virtual poster presentations, social mixers, or virtual spaces where participants' avatars can spontaneously interact, much like in casual hallway encounters.

Designing meetings with cultural evolutionary processes in mind highlights diversity and equitable participation as the basis for innovative and collaborative research environments needed to address complex scientific problems.
